I've been a loyal T-Mobile customer since 2016, back when they rolled out the T-Mobile ONE plan. I've been getting a military discount with them this whole time, but even with that discount, my bill eventually ballooned to $113 a month thanks to T-Mobile's price hikes. I'd had enough, so I started looking for cheaper alternatives. Couple that with the fact that this year's iPhone 18 Pro costs at least $100 more, and I figured if I'm going to get a new phone anyway, saving some money on my cellular bill might help offset the cost. So, I went MVNO shopping.

What is an MVNO?

MVNO stands for "Mobile Virtual Network Operator." Simply put, an MVNO is a wireless carrier that doesn't actually own a nationwide cellular network itself. Instead of building their own network, they buy capacity from one of the major carriers (AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon) and resell that service to their own customers. Think of them as middlemen for wireless networks.

That means switching to an MVNO doesn't necessarily mean giving up your current network. For example, Mint Mobile uses T-Mobile's network, Visible uses Verizon's, and US Mobile lets customers choose between any of the Big Three. For this article, I'll be focusing on those three MVNOs because they're the ones I researched most thoroughly before leaving T-Mobile, but there are plenty of other options out there.

At its core, an MVNO gives you another way to purchase cellular service without going directly to the company that owns the network.

Why are MVNOs cheaper? What are the "catches"?

If an MVNO can use the exact same cellular network as AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon, how can they charge so much less? In short, MVNOs don't shoulder all the costs of running a nationwide wireless carrier. They don't have to build and maintain their own networks, many operate primarily online without maintaining physical retail stores, and they typically have much smaller staffs. The cost savings can then be passed back to customers through lower monthly rates.

MVNO plans tend to be more bare-bones, lacking many of the "perks" and extras common with traditional carriers. Depending on the carrier and plan, you might not get free streaming services or other benefits traditional carriers use to retain customers. However, if you actually want those "free" perks, the money you save by going with an MVNO can easily cover the cost of paying for them yourself.

I've been there myself. I always looked forward to T-Mobile's included MLB.TV subscription, which I used every season, but I never watch Netflix, so the "Netflix on Us" benefit was wasted on me. Even if I wanted both Netflix and MLB.TV, I could simply pay for those subscriptions myself and still come out ahead after factoring in the savings from switching to an MVNO. At the end of the day, I want reliable, affordable cellular service, and I don't need T-Mobile throwing in a bunch of extras just to let me use their network.

The "catches" aren't necessarily worse service, but rather less of what you're paying for. What exactly you're giving up depends on the MVNO and plan you choose. Video streaming might be limited to lower resolutions, high-speed or premium data allowances will vary, and network prioritization may be different. I have fast Wi-Fi at home, and I rarely go to concerts or sporting events where things are "congested," so for everyday use, network prioritization isn't a huge deal for me. But I do travel internationally occasionally, so international data is an important consideration. Some MVNOs include international data and texting, some charge extra for it, or offer limited coverage when you leave the US.

Then there are some less obvious differences, particularly when buying a new iPhone. Apple Card Monthly Installments and the iPhone Upgrade Program aren't available if your carrier is an MVNO. If you want to use either of those options, you're stuck choosing AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon. Practically speaking, if you buy your iPhone directly from Apple, you'll likely need to pay for it upfront. Traditional major carriers can also offer substantial trade-in credits or other incentives, which generally aren't available from MVNOs. Apple Watch support isn't universal either, so if you have a cellular Apple Watch, you'll want to pay attention to that.

Finally, many MVNOs rely primarily on phone and online customer support rather than in-person retail locations. I consider myself half a techie, and I have no desire to stand in line at a store waiting for help. And in my experience, store salespeople just end up calling the same number I'd be calling anyway, so doing it from home works just as well, which makes this a non-issue for me.

Most importantly, these aren't universal MVNO problems. Restrictions vary by carrier and plan, so it's worth examining exactly what you're getting before making the switch.

Three MVNOs worth considering

After deciding to leave T-Mobile, I started looking at my other options. Verizon and AT&T's postpaid plans were more expensive than what I was already paying, so the other two major carriers were immediately out. I ultimately narrowed my search to US Mobile, Mint Mobile, and Visible. Each had something that appealed to me, and all could significantly cut my monthly communications spending without forcing me off a major carrier's network.

US Mobile is arguably the most flexible of the three, and it's the one I ultimately switched to from T-Mobile. That doesn't mean it's necessarily the best fit for you, or even the best MVNO of the bunch — just the best fit for my needs.

US Mobile wasn't actually my first choice initially. It was a company I'd never heard of until I started researching MVNOs. But the more I looked into it, the more impressed I became. Here's why: US Mobile offers service on all three major US networks, letting customers choose whichever works best for them. It also offers a Multi-Network add-on that can activate two networks on the same iPhone simultaneously, without needing a second phone number. Both networks are tied to the same line, and your iPhone can seamlessly use whichever network is performing better for calls and data. That means if T-Mobile works great at your office but Verizon is better at home, you can have the best of both worlds without carrying two phones or managing two numbers. This feature costs extra from US Mobile, and I don't need it, but it's a pretty neat option to have.

I recently moved, and I was curious how Verizon's coverage would compare to T-Mobile's around my new place, so I decided to test both networks. I set my wife's iPhone to US Mobile's Light Speed network (that's T-Mobile), and my iPhone to Warp (that's Verizon), so we could see the difference firsthand. Turns out Verizon is significantly better in our area, so switching to US Mobile ended up being a win-win: better coverage and much cheaper service.

Mint Mobile was actually my first choice, since it's a T-Mobile company, meaning I could stay on the network I knew but pay a lot less. What I didn't like was that it doesn't include international data. My wife and I love taking cruises, and travel is a big part of our lives, so having cellular data outside the US is important to us. Mint does offer international data, but it costs extra and would quickly eat into the savings. I also didn't like that taxes and fees are charged separately.

Visible is similarly straightforward, but it only runs on Verizon's network. My biggest hesitation with Visible was Verizon's coverage in my area. I'd been a T-Mobile customer for nearly a decade, so I knew exactly what T-Mobile's network performance was like, but I had no idea what to expect from Verizon. That was actually the only reason I ultimately chose US Mobile over Visible, since US Mobile let me try Verizon's network, and if it didn't work out, I still had T-Mobile and AT&T as backups. Visible's top unlimited plan even includes a free cellular Apple Watch line, which is a pretty appealing perk. (US Mobile offers the same perk on its top plan when using Warp, which is Verizon's network.)

What do you need to switch?

Switching to an MVNO was even easier than I expected. My wife and I kept our existing iPhones, and it took about ten minutes to move both lines from T-Mobile to US Mobile. I didn't even have to leave the couch. You'll need an unlocked, compatible iPhone (or Android phone, but I'm focusing on iPhone here), along with some information from your current carrier. If you want to keep your existing phone number, just make sure you don't cancel your old service before the number is ported over.

Here's what you'll need to switch:

  • Account number from your current carrier
  • Transfer PIN
  • An unlocked, compatible iPhone
  • A new eSIM
  • A little patience

In preparation for the switch, I prepaid US Mobile for two unlimited lines annually. My wife doesn't have a cellular Apple Watch and doesn't care about video quality, so she opted for US Mobile's Unlimited Starter plan, saving $100 compared to the Unlimited Premium plan I chose. Two lines plus an Apple Watch line came to $500 annually, compared to the $1,356 a year I was paying T-Mobile for two lines with no Apple Watch service. (Again, that price already includes the military discount!)

Getting a transfer PIN from T-Mobile was straightforward — I was half-expecting it to be hidden behind some convoluted process, but it wasn't. Here are the relevant guides for Verizon and AT&T.

After connecting my iPhone to Wi-Fi, US Mobile emailed me a new eSIM, and installation was as simple as clicking a button in the email and following the on-screen prompts. My wife's iPhone followed the same process. The only extra step was setting up my Apple Watch, which I was able to handle easily through the US Mobile app.

Why I'm sticking with MVNO

Same coverage, more savings: When I weigh the trade-offs against the money I'm saving, it's absolutely worth it. I have fast Wi-Fi at home, so cellular data isn't a huge concern for me (though in terms of speed tests, US Mobile is just as fast as T-Mobile ever was). What matters most is having strong, reliable cellular signal when I'm away from Wi-Fi, especially for calls and texts.

No long-term contracts: Most carriers have already done away with traditional contract plans in favor of device installment plans, which effectively achieve the same thing — you have to finish paying off the device before you can leave. I've always bought my iPhones directly from Apple because I appreciate the freedom of having an unlocked device, but I also appreciate that US Mobile, Mint, and Visible don't require contracts.

Easy to switch: Most MVNOs let you pay monthly, so there's no long-term contract to sign. If one carrier is running a promotion one month and another has a better deal the next, switching is quick and easy. Prepaid accounts also don't require credit checks, meaning your credit score won't take a hit from a carrier inquiry the way it might with a postpaid account, and you won't be denied service even if your credit is less than stellar. My credit is fine, but I didn't want to take a hard hit just for switching from T-Mobile to Verizon.

Annual payment saves more: The trade-off for that flexibility is that you'll save even more if you're willing to prepay for a full year of service. Most MVNOs offer significant discounts for annual plans, so you're giving up some of the freedom to switch whenever you want in exchange for a lower overall price.

No surprise charges: As I mentioned earlier, my wife and I love taking cruises. If you've ever been on a ship and forgot to put your iPhone in airplane mode, only to have it connect to the ship's cellular network, you know the shock of a potentially massive bill. With a prepaid plan, I don't have to worry about accidentally racking up an enormous roaming charge. If international roaming isn't included in the plan, my phone simply won't connect to foreign networks, so I won't get charged. US Mobile's plans also include taxes and fees, so the price listed is exactly what you pay.

Switching to an MVNO isn't just about finding the cheapest service — it's about getting the service I actually want without paying for things I don't need or want. So far, I haven't felt like I've missed out on anything that matters to me (though I know I'll definitely miss that free MLB.TV subscription). In fact, I've gained an Apple Watch line I didn't have before, while spending less overall. I've got the same iPhone, the same phone number, and on US Mobile's Warp (Verizon) network, coverage in my area is actually better than before — and if I find a better option down the road, I can switch again whenever I want.

Your priorities might be different from mine, and an MVNO isn't necessarily the right choice for everyone. But if you're paying a lot for cellular service right now and haven't considered an MVNO, it's worth a look. You might be surprised at how little you're actually giving up.
